extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (epistemology, logic, philosophy of science)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and arguments for assessing whether axioms/‘necessary truths’ are a priori or derived from experience; discusses tests (chronology, conceivability, mental intuition), objections, and historical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronological priority as evidence of a priori origin
rubrics_metrics.description: If we can prove chronologically that we have the conviction so early in infancy as to be anterior to those impressions on the senses, then the conviction would be a priori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes this would support an a priori origin but also observes that such chronological proof "cannot be proved; the point being too far back to be within the reach of memory, and too obscure for external observation."

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought-intuition (imaginary inspection) vs. sensory experience
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proposition is 'seen to be true by merely thinking of [the objects]' rather than by actual trial or sensory inspection, this is taken as an indication that its ground is mental (a priori) rather than experiential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by: two straight lines cannot inclose a space — we allegedly recognize this by thinking of straight lines without having seen one. Counterpoint: the distinction between 'imaginary looking' and 'real looking' is examined and challenged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental images as experimental evidence when faithful
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometrical forms can be 'painted in the imagination with a distinctness equal to reality' so that mental pictures, if sufficiently accurate, 'exhibit of course all the properties which would be manifested by the realities' and are fit subjects of geometrical experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This makes apparent 'intuition' still an induction from observation, but only on the condition that we have earlier learned by experience that our mental images faithfully represent external reality (see separate criterion on prior empirical validation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of prior empirical validation of mental images
rubrics_metrics.description: We should not be authorized to substitute observation of the image in our mind for observation of the reality 'if we had not learnt by long continued experience that all the properties of the reality are faithfully represented in the image.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus mental or imagined inspection counts as evidence only when long experience justifies treating mental representations as equivalent to perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconceivability of negation as definition of necessary truths
rubrics_metrics.description: A necessary truth is one 'the negation of which is not only false, but inconceivable' — 'we cannot, even by an effort of imagination... conceive the reverse of that which is asserted.' (Whewell's formulation)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author reports this as the opposing view he addresses and then critiques this criterion's reliability (see 'association influences conceivability').

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of empirical induction for establishing necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience consists of a limited number of observations; however numerous, they 'can show nothing with regard to the infinite number of cases in which the experiment has not been made' and therefore cannot, by themselves, supply necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard objection from proponents of a priori necessity; the text presents it so the reader can weigh whether it actually entails that axioms are non-empirical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof on advocates of a priori origin
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of proof lies upon advocates of the contrary opinion: 'it is for them to point out some fact, inconsistent with the supposition that this part of our knowledge of nature is derived from the same sources as every other part.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a methodological standard: proponents of a distinct (a priori) source must cite facts incompatible with an empirical/inductive origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association and past mental history determine conceivability
rubrics_metrics.description: Our capacity or incapacity of conceiving a thing 'depends upon the past history and habits of our own minds' — repeated association can render certain separations of ideas inconceivable even though they are possible in themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's central critique of the 'inconceivability' test: inability to conceive a negation is often accidental and produced by habit, not proof of impossibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical counterexamples: formerly inconceivable propositions become conceivable
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical scientific shifts (e.g., antipodes, Newtonian gravity, laws of motion, chemical combination) show that propositions once regarded as inconceivable or paradoxical were later conceived and accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such historical examples to caution against treating present inconceivability as evidence of metaphysical necessity; they illustrate how association and habit change judgment over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagined extrapolation with empirical grounding when direct observation is impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where direct observation is unattainable (e.g., following lines to infinity), we can imagine the necessary appearance at a finite hypothesized point and rely on that imagination because of prior experience linking such images to reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supports treating some geometric 'intuition' as inductive reasoning based on mental experimentation, not evidence of a distinct a priori faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-evidence may be a product of later establishment and habit
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions discovered gradually and by effort, when once established, 'appear so self-evident that... it would have been impossible to conceive that they had not been recognised from the first' — self-evidence can therefore be an effect of historical induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution: do not infer original necessity from present self-evidence; the felt necessity may be retrospective, produced by repetition and acceptance.
